title: K-th Ordering of One to N
statement:
Write every ordering of the digits 1 to n as a string and sort the strings in dictionary order. For n = 3 the list is "123", "132", "213", "231", "312", "321".

Return the k-th string in that list, counting from 1.

examples.why: The fourth string in the list above.
Each first digit owns a block of 3! = 6 strings. k = 7 is the first string of the second block, which starts with 2. Treating k as 0-based would land one string too far.
Blocks of 6: k = 17 is in the third block (first digit 3) at position 5. Among 1, 2, 4, blocks of 2 put it in the third (digit 4) at position 1, leaving "12".

hints: How many strings start with the digit 1? With 2?
Each possible first digit owns a block of (n − 1)! strings. Which block holds k?
Convert to 0-based (k − 1). The first digit is the item at index (k − 1) / (n − 1)! in the list of unused digits; keep the remainder and repeat with (n − 2)!, and so on.

explain.intuition:
Sorted orderings come in blocks. With n digits, all orderings that start with the smallest digit come first, and there are (n − 1)! of them. Then come the (n − 1)! that start with the next digit, and so on. So dividing by (n − 1)! tells you the first digit directly, without listing anything.

After picking it, the remainder is the position inside that block, which is again a sorted list of orderings of the remaining digits. Repeat with (n − 2)!. This is the factorial number system: k − 1 written with factorial place values.
steps: Make a list of unused digits [1, 2, …, n] and set idx = k − 1.
For i from n − 1 down to 0: let block = i!.
Take the digit at position floor(idx / block) of the unused list, append it to the answer and remove it from the list.
pitfalls: Dividing k instead of k − 1. The first string of each block then maps to the previous block.
Forgetting to remove a used digit from the list, so a digit appears twice.
Generating all n! orderings first. It works for n = 9 but is far slower and misses the point.

solutions.title: Step to the next ordering k − 1 times
solutions.idea: Start from 123…n and apply the standard next-permutation step k − 1 times.

solutions.title: Factorial blocks
solutions.idea: Each first digit owns (n − 1)! orderings, so integer division by the block size picks each digit in turn.

followups: Go the other way: given an ordering, return its 1-based rank in the sorted list.
If n could be 100 000, how would you make removing the chosen digit faster than O(n)? (Hint: a Fenwick tree.)
